title: Bulk fermentation, reading the dough, not the clock
subtitle: The first rise in sourdough bread and why timing is a guide, not a rule
excerpt: Bulk fermentation is the first long rise of sourdough dough after mixing. The dough ferments as a single mass, building flavour and structure. Temperature and starter strength control how long it takes, which is why watching the dough matters more than watching the clock.
sourceNotes: Bulk fermentation guidance draws on contemporary sourdough baking practice. The relationship between dough temperature, fermentation time, and final crumb structure is well-established in practical sourdough literature. The dough-temperature-rise target (50 to 75% volume increase) is a widely used benchmark.

glossaryTerms.definition: The first fermentation stage of sourdough bread, during which the entire batch of dough rises together. The process builds flavour from organic acids and develops gluten strength through fermentation gases.
Stretching a small piece of dough thin enough to see light through without it tearing. It indicates sufficient gluten development.
Dough that has fermented beyond its peak. It collapses when scored, bakes flat, and produces a dense, gummy crumb.

content.text: starts the moment you mix flour, water, starter, and salt. The dough ferments as a single mass until it has risen by 50 to 75% and feels light, airy, and slightly tacky. At 21°C with a healthy starter, this typically takes 4 to 6 hours. A warmer kitchen shortens the window; a cold one lengthens it.

Mark the side of the bowl with tape at the start. Bulk is complete when the dough has risen by 50 to 75% of its original volume and shows a domed, slightly jiggly surface. Pull a small piece and perform the
: stretch it gently between your fingers. If it becomes translucent without tearing, gluten development is sufficient.

A dough at 24°C ferments twice as fast as one at 18°C. If your kitchen is warm, check the dough at 3 hours. If it is cool, plan for 6 to 8 hours. The timing on any sourdough recipe is a guide calibrated to a specific temperature; use it as a starting point, not a hard rule.
Underfermented dough is dense and tears when you try to shape it. The loaf bakes tight and dense.
dough is sticky, slumps in the hand, and produces a flat, gummy bake. Somewhere between the two is the sweet spot: the dough holds its shape when you fold it but has enough gas to feel pillowy.

Most sourdough recipes include three or four sets of stretch and fold during bulk, typically at 30-minute intervals in the first two hours. Each set builds strength and redistributes the culture through the dough. After the folds, leave the dough alone to rise undisturbed.

Many experienced bakers use 50% volume increase as their bulk endpoint rather than time. Mark the bowl, watch the dough, and shape when it reaches the mark. This adapts automatically to your kitchen temperature and starter strength.
